parsed.explanation: No criminalisation of trans identity or same-sex conduct has ever existed, and there is no documented trans-specific border friction or entry restriction. However, the combined regime documents: exclusion from establishments with 'little or no legal consequence' (everyday traveller-facing hostility with thin national recourse); scattered lethal violence with an official transfemicide 'pattern' finding, raw counts only; two narrow local dress/cross-dressing ordinances of undocumented enforcement; and, if detained, birth-sex placement in male dormitories with mandatory head-shaving and gang-mediated safety — a tier-1 state exposure with no documented remedy. National protections are a patchwork (nine provinces, 32 cities); slur/harassment statutes and positive state responses (NHRC, 198-0 lower-house vote, mayoral apology) partially offset but do not cure the custody and service-refusal gaps.

entry_documents.exposure: No trans-specific entry rule or document-mismatch friction documented. No legal gender recognition exists, but that is resident-facing; the visitor's home passport governs.
entry_documents.protection: Same-sex relations and trans identity never criminalised; 2026 travel score rates capital 62/100 for trans travellers ('Exercise Caution'), not a denial-of-entry profile.
entry_documents.interaction: Document discrepancy, if any, would interact with general inspection only; no dossier evidence of escalation to fraud or morality charges.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: If detained, transgender women are housed by birth sex in ordinary male dormitories with mandatory head-shaving, safety dependent on inmate hierarchies, and gang 'weddings' used as protection against abuse. A southern jail annex segregates LGBT detainees 'to prevent abuse'. No national placement rule exists; practice varies by facility.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: One facility's annex practice is a partial protective response; no documented remedy for male-dorm placement, head-shaving, or abuse.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A street offence, assembly charge (Pride arrests documented 2020), or the local dress ordinance could move a visitor into this custody system with no placement override.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: A southern city's 2004 ordinance bans men appearing in female attire/makeup/earrings; a 2019 municipal ordinance bans cross-dressing for members of a religious community under imprisonment. Gender-diverse people are excluded from public and private spaces with little legal consequence.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Nine provinces and 32+ municipalities prohibit SOGI discrimination; enforcement of the two hostile ordinances is not documented anywhere in the record.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Local hostility operates where national law is silent; a visitor's exposure varies sharply by locality, and the hostile ordinances are geographically narrow.

care_services.exposure: No documented denial of emergency or routine care to trans visitors.
care_services.protection: Statute prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, SOGI; anti-bullying rules list SOGI; one city's 2023 right-to-care card lets registered LGBTQ couples make medical decisions for each other.
care_services.interaction: Care-seeking out a traveller to staff is an open question; the right-to-care card requires registration the visitor is unlikely to hold.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Police arrested at least 20 Pride participants in 2020 under public-assembly and communicable-disease statutes (no violence alleged). No documented police campaign targeting trans presentation specifically.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Slur/harassment statutes (women's statute, safe spaces statute, social workers' statute) impose fines, short detention and sensitivity seminars for transphobic abuse; national human rights commission condemns killings but lacks enforcement power.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Assembly enforcement could reach a trans visitor joining a Pride event; harassment statutes give some recourse if police cooperate.

minors_guardians.exposure: School-level bullying/discrimination documented in a 2017 report; family conversion practices against LGBTQ teenagers of a religious group (resident-sphere, but relevant to a minor visiting relatives). Draft recognition bill would allow minors to choose markers — not yet law.
minors_guardians.protection: National education policy requires gender-stereotype review and Pride observance; uniform rules allow gender-identity-matching dress since 2016.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling minor outed in school or community settings faces hostility with only patchwork local protection; no documented institutional placement rule for minors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Two trans women killed on the same day in June 2025; killings reported since 2012 including by armed groups in one southern city; drag performer struck on stage April 2024; NHRC cites a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'. Counts only, no denominator; no organised state targeting documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Positive state responses: mayoral public apology after the stage attack, NHRC condemnation, equality bill passed lower house 198-0; a perpetrator was arrested in the May 2025 rape of a trans woman.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Scattered incidents (tier 4) with thin everyday recourse for service refusal; violence is public-borne, not state-directed.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No national equality statute (bill stalled 25 years, rejected 2022); human rights commission investigates but cannot enforce; exclusion from premises carries little consequence; enforcement of hostile local ordinances undocumented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Patchwork provincial/city SOGI ordinances, slur statutes, HIV-discrimination statute, professional-responsibility rules for lawyers; functioning legislature and courts evidenced by ongoing bill process.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Whether remedies work for a short-stay visitor outside ordinance localities is an open question; absence of national law leaves gaps unfilled where local ordinances are absent.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.25-C combines birth-sex prison placement with a statute criminalising cross-dressing in administrative buildings enabling visitor arrests. This dossier shares the custody exposure but lacks any national criminalisation of dress — its two hostile ordinances are local, narrow, and of undocumented enforcement. Higher than 0.25-C.

0.45-C has identity-verification portals flagging mismatches affecting jobs and leases plus a morality ordinance with fines and administrative holds. This dossier has comparable thin-recourse societal exclusion and local morality ordinances, but no routine identity-verification infrastructure and no documented administrative detention of visitors; offset by real statutory protections. Similar tier, slightly higher.

0.55-B is discretionary secondary screening ending in administrative refusal, with written reasons and appeals. This dossier has no documented border friction (better) but worse downstream features: documented lethal violence, an official transfemicide pattern finding, and birth-sex custody with head-shaving and no remedy. Roughly level, marginally lower.

parsed.synthesis: The regime is one of no criminalisation but weak national protection and real documented harms. Everyday traveller exposure is service refusal and social hostility with patchwork, locality-dependent remedies — thin but not absent recourse. Street violence is documented but scattered, unorganised, and met with positive state responses (NHRC, mayoral apology, arrest of a perpetrator), so it reads as tier-4 severity rather than a campaign. The heaviest feature is custody: any detention places a trans woman by birth sex in male dormitories with mandatory head-shaving and inmate-mediated safety — a tier-1 state exposure no record shows being remedied, reachable via assembly charges or narrow local dress ordinances. Positive institutional signals (198-0 vote, military inclusion since 2017, slur statutes, right-to-care card) are genuine but do not touch custody or guarantee service access. Net: Elevated Risk, low-middle.
